syllabi: What a marine or naval engineering technician on the electrical path uses of digital electronics: the public apprenticeship standards on the Institute for Apprenticeships site for a Marine engineer, Naval engineering technician (or nearest), Engineering technician (electrical or electronic) and Maintenance and operations engineering technician; the STCW Code Table A-III/6 (electro-technical officer) competence lines on electronics and computers; and the Pearson BTEC Level 3 and HNC unit lines on digital principles. Exact lines. Dan has no syllabi for his Navy courses ahead: plan against these and say where a choice is a guess
scope: Dan asked (3 Nov) for the Brilliant courses most relevant to his whole path; this is the first. He turned down Instrumentation and control (3 Nov), so this is a digital electronics course, not a controls course: no PID, no 4-20 mA loops, no sensors, and PLCs and alarm panels only as one-line examples. About eight lessons in about this order (the brief may merge or split): (1) Switches as logic: a contact is true or false; contacts in series are AND, in parallel are OR, a normally closed contact is NOT; starting from the control circuits he already wires (a start and stop circuit, interlocks). (2) Gates and truth tables: AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR, XOR and XNOR, their symbols (IEC and the common distinctive shapes), reading a gate circuit into a truth table and back. (3) Boolean algebra: the rules, De Morgan's laws, and simplifying an expression so a circuit needs fewer gates. (4) Designing from a truth table: sum of products, Karnaugh maps for three and four inputs, and building anything from NAND or NOR alone; a two-out-of-three majority vote as the worked design. (5) Binary and hexadecimal: place value in base 2 and 16, converting, how many states n bits give (2 to the n), signed numbers by two's complement, BCD in one line. (6) Adding with gates: the half adder, the full adder, a ripple-carry adder, overflow, and subtraction by two's complement. (7) Memory: feedback makes a latch (the SR latch from two NORs, set beside the seal-in contact of a motor starter), the gated latch, the D and JK flip-flops, the clock and edge triggering. (8) Counters, registers and conversion: a counter from flip-flops, dividing a frequency, a shift register, then digital to analogue and analogue to digital in outline (resolution as range over 2 to the n, the step size in volts, sampling fast enough). Each lesson opens with a puzzle he can feel his way through, then the rule, then typed-answer puzzles he works on paper. Interactives where he flips inputs and watches outputs, wires gates, and steps a clock. Examples from electrical plant in general (a pump's start permissive, a generator breaker's close interlock, a two-out-of-three sensor vote, a running-hours counter, a digital meter's resolution); never claim how the Navy or a boat does it, and never touch reactor protection
